analysis.one_liner: Taxes unrealized investment gains when assets are given away or left to heirs, with a $1 million exclusion.
analysis.headline: The bill never got past its referral to the House Ways and Means Committee on March 29, 2021; it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax law, when someone dies holding stock or other investments that have grown in value, the gain is never taxed: the heirs inherit the property with its value reset, and the capital gain disappears forever. This bill would treat those assets as sold at death, taxing the gain like any other sale — but only above a $1 million exclusion per person, with extra time to pay and reduced interest for illiquid assets. It would have applied to gifts and deaths after the end of 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit in two ways. The tax would fall almost entirely on very large estates, since the first $1 million of gain at death (adjusted for inflation) is excluded, and gifts under the annual gift-tax exclusion are not counted. The revenue would come from wealth that currently escapes income tax permanently, easing pressure on everyone else's taxes or funding public services. Family businesses and illiquid assets get relief through the option to pay over up to seven years at a reduced interest rate.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would tax capital gains above $1 million (indexed for inflation) that are currently excluded forever under the 'step-up in basis' rule, which resets the value of inherited property so no income tax is ever owed on the growth.
Gifts under the annual exclusion and transfers to a U.S.-citizen spouse or to charities would not be taxed, keeping the tax focused on very large transfers.
Heirs facing a large tax on illiquid assets like a family business could elect to pay in two to seven equal annual installments, at an interest rate equal to 45 percent of the standard rate.

New reporting requirements would require executors and gift-givers to report the value and basis of transferred property to the IRS, closing an information gap the current no-tax regime never needed to fill.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy households holding large appreciated investment portfolios would owe capital gains tax at death or on large lifetime gifts. Wealth managers, private equity and hedge fund investors whose stakes have grown substantially would face tax on gains that under current law can pass to heirs untaxed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy households with large appreciated assets

drawbacks.text: Executors and families would face new appraisal and paperwork burdens: every covered gift or bequest would need a fair market value, a basis figure, and an information return filed with the IRS.

Heirs of illiquid assets — a closely held business, farmland, or a concentrated stock position — could owe tax on value they have not yet received as cash, which is the problem the bill's installment option addresses but does not eliminate.

The carve-outs are generous to certain interests: transfers to charities and to U.S.-citizen spouses escape the tax entirely, and dynasty trusts get a 30-year clock rather than immediate taxation, leaving planning avenues open.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a genuine gap — the largest investment fortunes can pass gains from a lifetime of appreciation through generations without any income tax ever being collected — and it protects typical families with the $1 million exclusion. Its main weaknesses are compliance friction for executors and liquidity pressure on heirs of illiquid businesses, which the installment plan softens but does not fully solve. As a revenue and fairness measure the design is sounder than a blanket tax on all unrealized gains, though the carve-outs leave room for continued planning by the best-advised.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Pascrell Jr. introduced the bill on March 29, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law.
Three House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The committee took no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.
Because it applied to transfers after December 31, 2021, its window to become law closed as the Congress ran out.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy families with large appreciated estates came out ahead: the step-up rule that lets them pass investment gains to heirs without any capital gains tax remained untouched, along with the planning industry built around it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken to measure party splits; all four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on [S4], while the Democratic-controlled committee simply never acted [S5].

industries.industry: Wealthy households with large appreciated estates
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to pass a lifetime of untaxed investment gains to heirs under the step-up rule, taxing gains above $1 million at death. Their interest in keeping the current rule runs directly against the broader tax base that must make up the revenue.

industries.industry: Private investment funds and their managers (private equity, hedge funds)
industries.note: Fund stakes and carried interests that have appreciated substantially would be treated as sold at death or on large gifts, forcing tax on gains that currently roll to heirs tax-free. Their preference for the status quo conflicts with ordinary taxpayers who cannot shelter gains this way.
The bill would shrink demand for step-up-driven estate planning, but its new reporting rules and trust provisions create valuation and compliance work that requires professional help.
Transfers to charitable organizations would remain exempt from the deemed-sale tax, which could make charitable bequests relatively more attractive for wealthy households planning their estates.
